tasks.short: Check daily attendance, record absence and leave, correct clockings, work out overtime and send approved hours to payroll.

steps.what: Operators clock in and out at the time terminal
Supervisor checks the attendance list against the roster and notes absentees and late arrivals
Supervisor records sick calls and leave taken in a spreadsheet
Supervisor corrects missed clockings and works out overtime and shift allowances on the weekly sheet
Supervisor checks and approves the weekly hours
Supervisor e-mails the weekly hours file to payroll
Payroll administrator re-keys the hours into the payroll system

tasks.design: Configure the time and attendance system ({OTHER}) with the collective agreement's shift, break and overtime rules so hours and allowances are computed from clockings, and show the supervisor only exceptions: missed clockings, absentees, unplanned overtime. Absence and leave are recorded there with codes that flow to the {HCM}, and the approved week exports to the {PAYROLL} in its import format.
tasks.previous_blocker: Hours were rebuilt in spreadsheets because shift rules were never set up in the time system.
tasks.enabler_now: Time systems hold shift and overtime rules and export to payroll as standard configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Collective agreement rules have exceptions; any change to working-time rules or attendance registration needs works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing why someone is late or absent and handling it fairly.
tasks.altitude: The supervisor approves exceptions instead of building the weekly hours.

reach.learn: Whether imported hours cut corrections after the pay run.

evidence.claim: Time systems clock attendance at terminals, apply shift, break and overtime rules and export to payroll.
The works council must consent to rules on working and rest times, staff personal data and systems that can observe attendance or performance.

assumptions: Boundary: from clocking to hours in payroll; the pay run is outside.

Input contract: clockings by operators at terminals; shift and overtime rules set by HR from the collective agreement in the time system; absence codes agreed with HR; fallback is the weekly spreadsheet.
No new monitoring of operators is added beyond today's clocking.
Operator and payroll time is outside the supervisor's savings.
unknowns: Whether shift rules can be modelled in the current time system.
research_questions: How many payroll corrections per month come from hours today?

already_counted.description: Supervisor reviews the daily exception list.

incremental.description: Supervisor handles terminal failures and wrong codes.
HR keeps shift and overtime rules current with the collective agreement.

approvals.approved_version: The week's hours per employee as approved by the supervisor in s5; corrections after approval need a new approval.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Plants with many special shift arrangements that the time system cannot model keep spreadsheet corrections.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read work orders and schedules, work out material and setup requirements, collect output counts and compare actual with plan.

steps.what: Supervisor reads the day's work orders and production schedules from printouts
Supervisor works out material, tooling and setup requirements per order in a spreadsheet
Supervisor reads free-text order notes for special customer requirements

loop.input: Free-text notes on the day's work orders.
loop.output: A flag per order with the requirement type (packing, tolerance, labelling, material, other) and the quoted note text.
loop.check: The quoted text must appear in the note; the type must come from the fixed list; orders with any note but no flag are listed for the supervisor; the step changes nothing in the order.
loop.why_not_simpler: Notes are written freely by sales and customers; keyword rules miss special requirements phrased in other words.

steps.what: Supervisor collects output counts from machine displays and operator tally sheets
Supervisor compares outputs with current production estimates and finds causes of gaps
Supervisor decides adjustments: overtime, re-sequencing or escalation
Production planner revises the schedule on request

tasks.design: A planning board in the {OPS_SYSTEM} lists the day's orders and computes material, tooling and setup needs from the bill of materials and routing in the {ERP}; a bounded step flags special requirements in free-text order notes without changing anything. Machine counters and operator entries at manual stations feed a plan-versus-actual dashboard in {BI} with downtime reasons, so the supervisor reads gaps instead of collecting counts.
tasks.previous_blocker: Orders, counts and estimates lived on paper and in separate spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Production monitoring tools take machine counts and replace paper reports, and planning tools compute requirements from orders.
tasks.still_hard: Routing times are often wrong, so estimates mislead until engineering fixes them; line monitoring with operator login needs works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing on the floor why a line is behind and deciding what to change today.

ambition.what: Plan versus actual checked every hour instead of at the end of the shift.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor acts on gaps instead of compiling numbers; schedule changes stay with the planner.

reach.task: Set realistic run times per product
reach.learn: Whether actual counts show which routing times are wrong.

evidence.claim: A production monitoring tool replaced paper reports and spreadsheets at a building materials maker and runs in 23 factories in four countries; no numbers given.
A detailed planning tool schedules production from orders, linked to the ERP.
Systems that can observe attendance or performance, such as line monitoring with operator login, need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from reading orders to deciding adjustments; schedule changes by the planner are outside.

Input contract: bills of materials and routings kept by engineering in the {ERP}; machine counts from counters connected by maintenance; counts and downtime reasons at manual stations entered by operators on a terminal; fallback is tally sheets.
Counts are per machine and line, not per operator.
Planner and operator time is outside the supervisor's savings.
unknowns: How many machines have counters that can be connected.
How accurate routing times are today.
research_questions: Does hourly plan versus actual change how often lines finish the shift on target?

already_counted.description: Supervisor checks computed requirements for odd orders.
Supervisor checks counts from manual stations that look wrong.

incremental.description: Supervisor gets operators to enter downtime reasons.
Operators enter counts and downtime reasons at manual stations.
Engineering keeps routing times and bills of materials accurate.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Plants with old machines without counters keep tally sheets, and wrong routing times force manual estimates.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Sequence orders per machine, build the shift roster, assign operators by skill, brief the shift and re-plan after disruptions.

steps.what: Supervisor receives the weekly production plan from the planner
Supervisor sets production sequences per machine in a spreadsheet to limit setups
Supervisor builds work schedules for the shift from leave, absence and overtime
Supervisor makes assignments of operators to machines on the whiteboard
Supervisor briefs the team at the start of the shift
Supervisor re-plans after breakdowns or rush orders
Production planner confirms changes that affect delivery dates

tasks.design: A planning board in the {OPS_SYSTEM} proposes the sequence per machine from due dates, setup families and capacity, and recalculates after a breakdown or rush order. The roster pulls leave and absence from the time and attendance system ({OTHER}), and a skills matrix lists qualified operators per machine by fixed rules; the supervisor decides every sequence and assignment.
tasks.previous_blocker: Sequences and rosters were rebuilt by hand each day because setup families, skills and leave were in separate places.
tasks.enabler_now: Detailed planning tools schedule from orders linked to the ERP, and skills matrices and rosters are standard configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Setup families and run times must be right; a planning system with a poor interface was abandoned in one documented case.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which operator copes with which machine and what the team can handle today.

ambition.what: Sequences re-planned within minutes after every breakdown instead of once a day.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor adjusts proposals rather than building plans; delivery date changes stay with the planner.

reach.learn: Whether the planning board can reserve maintenance slots in the sequence.

evidence.claim: A detailed planning tool schedules production ahead from orders, linked to the ERP.
At a German screw conveyor maker, daily planning time fell by two hours a day and customer delivery time by 50% (vendor case, 2022).
Models that allocate tasks on behaviour or traits are high-risk; rule-based planning on machine capacity and qualifications is outside.
Rules on working times and systems observing staff need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the weekly plan to re-planning during the shift; the weekly plan and delivery promises are outside.

Input contract: setup families and run times kept by engineering; leave and absence from the time and attendance system recorded by supervisors and HR; skills matrix kept by the supervisor from training records; fallback is the spreadsheet and whiteboard.
Assignments use qualifications only, never performance data.
Planner time is outside the supervisor's savings.
unknowns: Whether setup families are defined today.
How often breakdowns force re-planning per week.
research_questions: How much setup time does a proposed sequence save against the supervisor's own?

already_counted.description: Supervisor reviews the proposed sequence before releasing it.
Supervisor checks the proposed qualified operators.

incremental.description: Supervisor keeps the skills matrix current.
Engineering keeps setup families and run times current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Job shops with one-off orders and no setup families gain little from proposed sequences.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Meet other supervisors daily, prepare the figures, hand over the shift, agree cross-department issues and follow them up.

steps.what: Supervisor gathers output, scrap and downtime figures from different sheets for the meeting
Supervisor writes the shift handover in the paper logbook

loop.input: The supervisor's brief notes and the shift's table of output, scrap and downtime per line.
loop.output: A shift report draft with a short commentary per line and open issues.
loop.check: Every number in the text must match the table; a mismatch stops the draft; each open issue must come from the notes or the issue board.
loop.stop: One draft per shift; on a stop the supervisor writes the commentary.
loop.why_not_simpler: Commentary explains why a line ran badly from free-text notes; the table alone does not say it.

steps.what: Supervisor confers with other supervisors in the daily production meeting
Supervisor calls or walks to other departments to coordinate operations: materials, maintenance, quality
Maintenance and quality supervisors act on the agreed issues
Supervisor chases open issues from earlier days

tasks.design: The plan-versus-actual dashboard in {BI} gives the meeting its figures; a shared issue board in the {WORKFLOW} tool records each cross-department issue with an owner and due date, so follow-up is a status check instead of a walk. The shift report is drafted from the supervisor's brief notes and the shift table, and stops if any number in the text differs from the table.
tasks.previous_blocker: Figures were gathered by hand and agreements lived in paper logbooks and memory.
tasks.enabler_now: Production monitoring replaces paper reports, and a scenario shows supervisors getting a shift report draft from brief notes.
tasks.still_hard: Coordination is negotiation between people with competing priorities; boards only help if everyone updates them.
tasks.human_edge: Getting maintenance and quality to act today because you know the people and the stakes.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; meetings start from shared figures and open issues.

reach.learn: Whether the shared issue board replaces their own action list.

evidence.claim: In a vendor scenario a supervisor gives brief notes and gets a shift report draft; no measured result.
A production monitoring tool replaced paper reports and spreadsheets across 23 factories; no numbers given.
Systems that can observe performance need works council consent; the board tracks issues, not people.

assumptions: Boundary: from preparing the meeting to following up agreed issues; the other departments' work is outside.
Input contract: shift table from the plan-versus-actual dashboard; issues entered with owner and due date by the supervisor who raises them; fallback is the logbook.
Other supervisors' time is outside this supervisor's savings.
The meeting itself does not change.
unknowns: Whether a dashboard with shift figures exists.
Number of cross-department issues per week.
research_questions: Do issues with a named owner and date close faster?

already_counted.description: Supervisor checks the drafted shift report before handing over.

incremental.description: Supervisor keeps own issues updated on the board.
Other supervisors update the issues they own.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: If other departments do not update the board, the supervisor goes back to walking and calling.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The production supervisor keeps the floor, the people and the decisions; hours, counts, sequences and reports become proposals and exceptions to check.
role.ambitious_version: A supervisor who re-plans within minutes after a breakdown and spends the shift on the floor rather than in spreadsheets.

job.title: First-Line Supervisors of Production and Operating Workers
